name: Niche perfume / sample decants

card.summary: Small vials of perfume sold so people can test pricey scents first; a shopping practice, not an appearance intervention.
card.note: Limited sourcing; authenticity of third-party decants is not covered by reviewed sources.

quick.overview:
Decants are small portions of perfume sold in vials so buyers can try a fragrance before committing to a full bottle. Niche perfumery refers to smaller, often pricier houses.

The practice is popular in fragrance communities; encyclopedic coverage is minimal.
quick.mechanism: A seller transfers liquid from a full bottle into a small container; the buyer wears it to judge the scent.
quick.risks: As with any fragrance, ingredients can cause skin allergy or breathing irritation in some people. Source and handling of decants vary by seller.

lead: Decants are small portions of a perfume transferred from a full bottle into a small spray vial, sold so buyers can wear a fragrance for days before committing to a full bottle. "Niche" perfumery refers to smaller houses that use selective distribution and target a narrower audience than mass-market designer releases.[2]

People use decants to build a signature scent, which is part of grooming and how a person is perceived. One retailer, Scento, argues that a brief in-store test misses how a fragrance develops and wears over several days and in different weather, and that decants let buyers sample several scents for the price of one bottle.[3] Its listed sizes are 2, 5 and 8 ml, with roughly 30, 75 and 120 sprays respectively.[3]

Niche perfumery gained a following in Europe and North America in the late 20th and early 21st centuries; Luca Turin and Tania Sanchez call L'Artisan Parfumeur, founded in 1976, the first niche firm.[2] Concentration terms help buyers compare products: parfum or extrait contains roughly 15 to 30 percent aromatic compounds, eau de parfum about 15 percent and eau de toilette 5 to 15 percent, though houses set their own concentrations.[1]

chain: Small vial lets you try an expensive fragrance for days
Choose a scent that suits your skin and style
angle.text: Decants let buyers test niche or expensive fragrances on their own skin before buying, so the scent they wear regularly is one they have chosen from experience.

paras: Natural perfume materials come from plants, animals, lichens and seaweed, while synthetics are produced by a small number of large companies.[1] Because scent labels such as eau de parfum are imprecise and can vary between houses, the same name can denote different strengths.[1]

Wikipedia's niche perfume article says niche houses make smaller batches than designer or celebrity fragrances, that the 1995 opening of the New York boutique Aedes de Venustas is cited as the start of a boom, and that luxury conglomerates bought many niche lines in the 2010s, blurring the line with designer brands.[2]

Scento says its decants are hand-filled from sealed bottles obtained from authorised European retailers, and lists advantages including lower upfront spend, more realistic testing over several days, fewer unworn full bottles and easy rotation by mood or season. It also acknowledges that decants usually cost more per millilitre than full bottles and lack the box and presentation of a sealed bottle.[3] These are seller statements; no independent data on authenticity or storage were found.

Fragrance is discussed alongside grooming and style as part of overall presentation, and decants come up as a way to try expensive scents without full-bottle purchases. Specific community sources were not available for citation.
Fragrance ingredients can trigger skin allergies, headaches and asthma reactions in some people.[1] Perfume contents are rarely disclosed in full, as companies cite trade secrets.[1]

timeline.event: L'Artisan Parfumeur is founded; Turin and Sanchez call it the first niche firm.[2]
Aedes de Venustas opens in New York, cited as the start of a niche boom.[2]
Estee Lauder buys Jo Malone London, an early niche acquisition by a luxury group.[2]
